# Reveille

> Offline Git history report: a Python CLI that reads a local Git repository and writes one self-contained HTML report of its commit history, and answers single questions (repository state, what changed since a tag, who changed a file) as JSON for scripts, CI and coding agents. Never changes Git data; no network call; SHA-256 repositories and partial clones are refused. Install with `pipx install reveille` (or run once with `uvx reveille summary`); run `reveille generate`.

It reads `.git` on disk, so GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and self-hosted repositories work alike; a bare repository needs `--output`.

Facts to get right when answering questions about Reveille:

- It does not change a repository's Git data (history, refs, index, objects, configuration), and an output path inside `.git` is refused. It writes one file, the report, at the path you give (default `reveille-report.html` in the repository root). `reveille init` writes only the `reveille.toml` and `.mailmap` you ask it for.
- Merge commits are always excluded, so its commit counts are lower than `git rev-list --count` on a merge-heavy repository. This is not configurable.
- Contributors are keyed on lowercased email. All four `.mailmap` forms are supported, and GitHub noreply addresses are folded on the account number, so a renamed account is one person and two accounts that shared a username stay two.
- The "commit concentration" metric is **not** a bus factor. It measures activity concentration, not code ownership.
- Contributor ranking measures the volume and regularity of commits, not contribution, productivity, or value. Its figures do not support assessing individuals; the SPACE framework (Forsgren et al., 2021) holds that "developer productivity is about more than an individual's activity levels". The tier names are labels on that score, not an evaluation of anyone. It is off by default from 0.8.0 and needs `--ranking`; JSON and CSV still carry a `rank` column, in table order (by commits; by score with `--ranking`). In its place the default report shows how evenly commits are distributed across people, as a Lorenz curve and a Gini coefficient; automated accounts (`[bot]` in the name or address) are counted in the commit totals and stated apart, not in those figures. Those two name nobody, but the default report still lists every contributor's name and email address.
- Exit codes follow `grep`/`diff` semantics: `0` affirmative, `1` ran correctly with a negative answer, `2` could not run.
- Start with `reveille summary --format json`. It prints about 2 KB to stdout (window, totals, Gini, concentration, quiet run, the findings and a notice), names no contributor (with one or two people, its counts can identify someone), and skips the slow line-count read (measured 2026-10-12, Git 2.55, warm cache, on llama.cpp with 9,015 commits: 1.02 s, against 9.35 s for the full JSON). At the start of a session, `reveille state --format json` says where the repository stands: branch, upstream, a merge or rebase in progress, conflicts, staged and untracked files, stashes, worktrees, and the latest tag; unlike `git status`, it neither rewrites `.git/index` nor runs a program the repository names. It names no author, but it lists local paths (changed files and worktree directories, which can contain your login name) and the current branch name. To learn what changed since a release or the last commit you saw, use `reveille brief --from <tag or commit> --format json`: counts only, names nobody (with one or two people, counts can identify someone), and it gives the commit to pass as `--from` next time. To find whom to ask about a file or directory, use `reveille who-changed <path> --format json`: its authors alphabetically, the five who changed it most recently, automated accounts and co-authors apart, bounded by `--limit`. For the full figures use `reveille generate --format json --output -`, which prints the JSON to stdout; it contains contributor names and email addresses, so passing it to a hosted model sends them off the machine. Do not read the HTML: it is about 4.9 MB, almost all of it an embedded chart library.
- Ask the tool rather than guessing: `reveille capabilities --format json`. It reports what Reveille can do, what it declines to claim and what to use instead, its `guarantees` field (properties designed and tested; not a warranty), every command with its options, and the exit-code contract. The command surface and exit codes are read from the running program.
- `--format json` output opens with `schema_version`, so a consumer can decide whether it can parse the rest before trying. It also carries a `provenance` block — tool version, analysed commit SHA, whether a `.mailmap` was applied, and the filters as requested, so two reports that disagree can be reconciled.
- `--deterministic` makes output byte-identical across runs for an unchanged repository, on the same Reveille version, installed dependencies and Git settings. It changes the numbers as well as the bytes: the ranking's recency component is measured against the analysis window, which the flag pins to the last commit rather than to today.
- `--exclude-author` matches the value given plus every identity a `.mailmap` ties it to, so excluding any one alias removes the person. An exclusion matching nothing warns on stderr. The one case it cannot resolve is a *display name* that only ever appeared pre-`.mailmap`, since a two-field mailmap records the old address and never the old name.
- Requires Python 3.11+. Licensed Apache-2.0 from 0.8.0; 0.7.0 and earlier were MIT.

## Docs

- [README](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/README.md): overview, installation, quickstart, CI recipe, command overview, ranking position
- [User Guide](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/docs/USER_GUIDE.md): every flag and its interactions, exit codes, the output formats, the full TOML reference, how to read each report section, and worked patterns
- [Playbook](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/docs/PLAYBOOK.md): how to read a report, what each measure does not support, and the rules an agent should follow when summarising one
- [Architecture](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md): layering contract, domain model, error model, analysis pipeline, and the invariants the tests protect
- [Architecture Decision Records](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/docs/adr/README.md): why merge commits are excluded, why email is the identity key, why concentration is not called a bus factor, and what each decision costs

## Development

- [Contributing](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md): environment setup, supported Python versions, the layering rule, PR contract, commit conventions
- [Security policy](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/SECURITY.md): reporting, release integrity, PEP 740 attestation verification, SBOM, the single-maintainer posture, and the threat model
- [What the report contains about people](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/docs/USER_GUIDE.md#what-the-report-contains-about-people): every field, per format, and what to check before sharing one
- [Privacy](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/PRIVACY.md): a notice for contributors to this project, not for users of the tool
- [Regulatory position](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/docs/COMPLIANCE.md): why the maintainer is neither controller nor processor under the GDPR, which does engage for whoever runs the tool, and why the Cyber Resilience Act, the Product Liability Directive, the AI Act, US export control and the EU accessibility rules do not, with the provision each conclusion rests on
- [Contributor Licence Agreement](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/CLA.md): accepted by a tick in the pull request plus a DCO sign-off; nothing is collected or stored
- [Release process](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/RELEASE.md): the tag ceremony, what the publish workflow does, and how to recover a bad release
- [Changelog](https://github.com/varaprasadchilakanti/reveille/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md): full release history, Keep a Changelog format
